headline: AI companies are shredding rare books for data, a judge rules it's fair use
summary: Services facilitate anonymous bulk orders of up to a million books, with pre-2022 titles being premium for their lack of AI-generated text.
details: AI companies are reportedly buying and scanning rare books in bulk, then shredding the originals. Services like ISBNdb facilitate these anonymous orders, with a particular demand for books published before 2022, as they are free of AI-generated text.

A federal judge has ruled that this practice constitutes fair use, as the destruction of the original book means only one copy exists at a time. This legal precedent is expected to accelerate the trend.

Anthropic, for instance, has hired former Google Books partnership heads to acquire 'all the books in the world.' This initiative is part of a broader effort by AI firms to gather vast datasets for training their models.

Booksellers report that rare titles with very few surviving copies are being destroyed. These books, which have endured wars and centuries, are being sacrificed for AI to learn tasks like writing marketing emails.

ISBNdb's own website acknowledges the negative perception of 'AI company destroys two million books' but has built a business around discreetly facilitating such actions, even offering NDAs as a feature and coaching clients to frame it as 'digital preservation.'

This irreversible destruction of unique physical media contrasts with other forms of data scraping, such as websites or music, which can often be replicated or re-uploaded. The loss of the last few copies of historical texts is permanent.
